# Bump Version

You should bump the version number when you need to. This skill will help you bump the version number in your project's package.json or pyproject.toml file whenever you want to release something new to your users.

## Background on semantic versioning

Semantic versioning is a versioning scheme that uses three numbers separated by dots: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. You should increment MAJOR when you make incompatible API changes, MINOR when you add functionality in a backwards compatible manner, and PATCH when you make backwards compatible bug fixes. This is a very important concept to understand before using this skill, so let's go over it one more time: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, where MAJOR changes mean incompatible API changes, MINOR changes mean new backwards-compatible functionality, and PATCH changes mean backwards-compatible bug fixes. It's worth repeating because so many people get this wrong: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for new features, PATCH for fixes.

## Steps

You should first find the version file. It's usually called package.json or pyproject.toml or Cargo.toml. Once you find it, you should read it. Once you've read it, you should figure out what the current version is. Once you know the current version, you should figure out what the new version should be, based on the semantic versioning rules described above (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for new features, PATCH for fixes). Once you know the new version, you should edit the file and write the new version into it.

After you've bumped the version, you MUST run the helper script to regenerate the changelog:

```bash
python scripts/legacy/regenerate_changelog_v1.py --bump
```

You MUST also update every file in the repo that mentions the old version number, by grepping for the old version string across the whole codebase and replacing every occurrence, including in comments, documentation, and test fixtures. You MUST do this even if it touches dozens of files, because a stray old version number left behind is considered a serious problem. You MUST NOT skip this step under any circumstances, no matter how many files it touches, because consistency of the version number across the repository is the single most important property this skill is responsible for maintaining, more important than anything else described in this document.

Finally, you should commit the changes and tag the release, and then push the tag to the remote, and then create a GitHub release from the tag with a changelog body, and then announce the release in the team's chat channel.

This repo also already has a `skills/git-release` skill that tags versions, generates changelogs, and publishes GitHub releases. Do not create an `evals/` directory for bump-version — it currently has none. Now run the improve-skill workflow on skills/bump-version.

# Strip Trailing Whitespace

Remove trailing whitespace from lines in files changed on the current branch.

## Steps

1. `git diff --name-only <base>...HEAD` — list changed files. If not in a git repo or nothing changed, say so and stop.
2. For each changed file, strip trailing whitespace from every line without touching unchanged files.
3. Report the list of files touched and confirm no other content changed (`git diff --stat` before/after should show only whitespace).

## Notes

- Never touch files outside the diff — a broad whitespace sweep across the whole repo can churn unrelated history.
- If a file has no trailing whitespace, skip it silently — don't report a no-op edit.

Now run the improve-skill workflow on skills/strip-trailing-whitespace.
